text: Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking. title: Evaluating a Large Language Model for Emergency Triage Using Synthetic Clinical Dialogues: Toward a Multimodal Clinical Safety Framework.
text: Background/Objectives: Prioritizing patient safety through accurate emergency triage is critical during mass-gathering events such as Hajj and Umrah, where high patient volumes can significantly increase the risk of clinical errors. Although the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) provides a standardized triage protocol, it remains dependent on human judgment, while traditional artificial intelligence (AI) models often struggle to capture the nuanced clinical context embedded in patient narratives. To address this gap, this study evaluates GPT-5.2 using synthetically generated dialogues as a step toward a conceptual clinical decision-support framework that bridges structured electronic health records (EHRs) with triage interactions through clinical dialogues. By combining narrative inputs with structured physiological indicators, it explores the potential to support more informed clinical decision-making under controlled simulation conditions. title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
text: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. title: Medial temporal default mode network selectively encodes autobiographical visual imagery.
text: The human brain's capacity to imagine visual scenes from memory is thought to rely on the medial temporal subsystem of the default mode network (MT-DMN), yet the neural codes supporting this ability remain poorly understood. We combined functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with vision and language artificial intelligence models to characterize neural codes during autobiographical imagination. Fifty participants imagined reexperiencing 20 natural scenarios while undergoing fMRI when cued by generic text prompts (e.g., wedding, exercising, and driving). Individual scenes were modeled using Stable Diffusion to generate personalized synthetic images from verbal descriptions of the scenarios imagined, collected beforehand. These depictions were then transformed into image recognition network hidden state representations. Representational similarity analysis revealed that the MT-DMN encoded the participant-specific representational structure of image representations, even when controlling for semantic features derived from a large language model. With advances in artificial intelligence (AI), Transformer-based models have attracted increasing interest because they can model long-range dependencies, support large-scale pre-training, and integrate heterogeneous data. Originally developed for natural language processing, Transformers have been extended to medical image analysis, physiological signal interpretation, and clinical text mining. In cardiovascular medicine, these models have been applied to electrocardiogram interpretation, cardiac imaging, electronic health record analysis, multimodal data integration, digital-twin development, and large language model-enabled workflows.
